item.title: sshcert-authorize
item.description:
sshd asks it, for each certificate login, which principals may log into the account. It answers with the account’s principals only if the certificate’s domain grant names this host; otherwise it answers nothing, and sshd refuses the certificate. It takes the arguments, flags, output and log format of GÉANT’s ssh-cert-authorize, and differs in what it refuses.

How sshd calls it 

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config
TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/efp-ssh-ca.pub
AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand /usr/local/bin/sshcert-authorize %u %k
AuthorizedPrincipalsCommandUser nobody
install -o root -g root -m 0755 sshcert-authorize /usr/local/bin/
echo login.example.org > /etc/ssh/cert-allowed-domain.conf

and, for each local account, the principals that may log into it, one per line, in /etc/ssh/auth_principals/<account>. sshd runs the command only from a path owned by root and writable by nobody else.

%u is the account being logged into. %k is the certificate, base64; a whole ssh-...-cert-v01@openssh.com BASE64 line is read too, and when the argument is absent the certificate is read from standard input. A third argument, when one is given (sshd’s %t), must be the certificate’s type, or the certificate is refused.

exit prints sshd
0 the account’s principals, one per line lets the certificate in if one of its principals is among them
1 nothing refuses it
2 nothing refuses it: the arguments were wrong

It does not check the signature, the CA or the validity dates

Nothing in the command verifies the certificate’s signature or its validity window: sshd, which trusts the CA through TrustedUserCAKeys, does that. The command decides one question, whether the certificate is meant for this host and this account.

What it refuses

In the order it checks:

  1. an account name that is empty, ., .., or holds /, \ or a NUL;
  2. a host with no domain configured, or one that is not a valid host name;
  3. a certificate that does not parse, a plain key, or a host certificate;
  4. a %t that is not the certificate’s type;
  5. with --krl, a certificate the list revokes, or every certificate when the list cannot be read or has expired;
  6. a domain grant that is present and malformed, whatever the flags;
  7. no domain grant at all, unless --allow-no-grant;
  8. a grant none of whose patterns matches any of the host’s names;
  9. an account with no principals file, or an empty one.

The host’s names are --domain, or the variable --domain-env names, or the lines of --domain-file (blank lines and # comments ignored; several lines are several names, any of which may match).

Against certificates signed by a test CA for the account alice, whose principals file lists a1b2c3@univ-example.fr, on a host called login.hpc.example.org:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.fr granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
INFO: action=authorized user=alice cert_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.fr"] server_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.fr"] domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
a1b2c3@univ-example.fr

The last line is the answer sshd reads; the lines before it are the log, here on standard error. A certificate granted other hosts:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-other-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1003 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.fr other host" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="domain not granted" grant=["*.elsewhere.example.net"] serial=1003 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg

A certificate with no grant:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-nogrant-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1002 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.fr no grant" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="no domain grant" serial=1002 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg

An account with no principals file, and a plain key:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals bob "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.fr granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
WARNING: action=denied user=bob domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="no principals file for the user" serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice.pub)"
WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="a ssh-ed25519 key, not a certificate"

Each of these exited 1, and printed nothing on standard output.

Why a certificate with no grant is refused

GÉANT’s ssh-cert-authorize lets a certificate with no domain grant through (“might be valid for non-domain-based auth”), and one whose grant it cannot parse, or that is empty. Then a site that trusts two CAs in TrustedUserCAKeys (the federation’s, and its own for staff, or a test CA) lets a certificate from the second CA in on every host, for any principal in a principals file, with no domain check at all. The domain filter is only a filter if a certificate that does not say where it may be used is refused.

A site that really wants GÉANT’s behaviour says so, and the command logs each time it applies it:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --allow-no-grant --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-nogrant-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1002 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.fr no grant" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
WARNING: action=no_grant_allowed user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1002 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
INFO: action=authorized user=alice cert_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.fr"] server_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.fr"] domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1002 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
a1b2c3@univ-example.fr

Even then, a grant that is present but malformed is refused.

--krl

RevokedKeys is sshd’s own check, made before the command runs, for every key and certificate, and it also revokes a CA key; prefer it. --krl FILE checks an OpenSSH KRL inside the command, and adds what sshd does not do: it refuses every certificate once the list has expired (its expires@go-authn.github.io extension, which sshd ignores), and every certificate when the list cannot be read. A list with no expiry is used without one.

Three runs: with the KRL authn-revokd writes, first a current one, then the fail-closed one it writes when the issuer’s list lapses; and last with --krl naming a file that does not exist:

$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --krl ../revokd/out/sshd.krl --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.fr granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
INFO: action=authorized user=alice cert_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.fr"] server_principals=["a1b2c3@univ-example.fr"] domain=login.hpc.example.org serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
a1b2c3@univ-example.fr
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --krl ../revokd/out/sshd.krl --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.fr granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="certificate revoked" serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
$ sshcert-authorize --syslog=false --krl missing.krl --domain-file cert-allowed-domain.conf --principals-dir auth_principals alice "$(cut -d' ' -f2 alice-cert.pub)"
INFO: action=cert_processed serial=1001 key_id="a1b2c3@univ-example.fr granted" extension=ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg
WARNING: action=denied user=alice domain=login.hpc.example.org reason="KRL unreadable: open missing.krl: no such file or directory" serial=1001 ca_fingerprint=SHA256:6gbNjRq4BYFximPaiHg3L5G01DO7ycES/Bx2Hg4Qkvg

The second run is refused because the fail-closed list revokes the certificate’s CA key: the check covers the certificate’s own key, its serial and key ID, and the key that signed it. The third is refused because the list cannot be read: no list is not taken to mean nothing revoked.

Flags 

$ sshcert-authorize -help
usage: sshcert-authorize [flags] USER [CERTIFICATE [KEYTYPE]]
An sshd AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand (%u %k) that refuses a certificate whose
ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org extension does not grant this host, or that has none.
-allow-no-grant
let in a certificate with no domain grant (GÉANT's behaviour); a malformed grant is still refused
-debug
log details
-domain string
the host's domain (overrides --domain-env and --domain-file)
-domain-env string
environment variable holding the host's domain
-domain-file string
file holding the host's domain, one name per line (default "/etc/ssh/cert-allowed-domain.conf")
-extension string
name of the domain-grant extension (default "ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org")
-krl string
refuse certificates this OpenSSH KRL revokes, and every certificate once it has expired or cannot be read
-principals-dir string
directory of principals files, one per user (default "/etc/ssh/auth_principals")
-syslog
log to syslog, facility AUTH (--syslog=false: to stderr) (default true)
-version
print the version and exit

Logs are key=value lines (action=cert_processed, action=denied, action=authorized, with serial and ca_fingerprint), to syslog, facility AUTH, by default. sshd discards the command’s standard error, so keep syslog on in production; --debug also writes everything to standard error. A value that comes from the client, such as the account name, is quoted when it holds a space, =, a quote or a control character, so it cannot forge a log field.

-version prints the module version, in a release binary and in one built by go install alike:

$ go install github.com/go-authn/sshcert/cmd/sshcert-authorize@v0.1.5
$ sshcert-authorize -version
sshcert-authorize v0.1.5

Before v0.1.5, a binary from go install printed sshcert-authorize dev.

item.title: sshcert
item.description:
A certificate from a federation’s CA is not, by itself, permission for every host that trusts that CA. The EuroHPC Federation Platform’s SSH CA writes the hosts a certificate is meant for into an extension, ssh-domain-grant@core.aai.geant.org, and sshd ignores it. go-authn/sshcert reads and writes that extension, and its command, sshcert-authorize, is what sshd runs to enforce it. Pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0. These pages describe v0.1.5.

$ go install github.com/go-authn/sshcert/cmd/sshcert-authorize@v0.1.5
$ sshcert-authorize -version
sshcert-authorize v0.1.5
sshcert-authorize the AuthorizedPrincipalsCommand: what it checks, what it refuses, and how sshd calls it

The extension

Its data is a compact JSON array of host patterns, ["login.example.org"]. A * matches one or more characters within a single label, and names compare without case:

pattern matches does not match
login.example.org login.example.org, LOGIN.example.org www.login.example.org
*.example.org a.example.org example.org, a.b.example.org
prod-*.example.org prod-1.example.org prod-.example.org
*.*.example.org a.b.example.org a.example.org

The reading is strict: only what the encoder writes is accepted. No whitespace, nothing after ], no JSON escapes, no duplicates, at most 64 patterns, each made of letters, digits, hyphens and *, in labels of 1 to 63 bytes, at most 253 bytes, and no * in the rightmost label. null, objects, numbers and nested arrays are refused. [] is accepted, and grants no host.

A grant that is present and malformed is never reported as absent. That difference is the whole point of the command.

Who uses it

  • authn-bridge writes the extension for a client’s ssh_domain_grants, after checking each pattern with this package’s ValidatePattern.
  • go-fileshare’s SFTP server reads it with ssh_domains, and refuses a certificate with no grant unless ssh_accept_ungranted is set.
  • sshcert-authorize is the same check for a plain sshd.
